chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim, they said: We asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

about the prayer of the eclipse, how many rak'ahs are there in it and how do we pray it? He said: 'It is ten rak'ahs and four prostrations. You begin the prayer with a takbir, and bow with a takbir, and raise your head with a takbir, except in the fifth one in which you prostrate, so you say 'Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah', and you make du'a (qunut) in every two rak'ahs before the bowing, and you prolong the qunut, bowing, and prostration according to the length of the recitation, bowing, and prostration. So when you finish before the eclipse clears, sit and supplicate to Allah until it clears. If it clears before you finish your prayer, then complete what remains. You recite aloud.'

I said: How is the recitation in it? He said: 'If you recite a surah in every rak'ah, then recite Fatihat al-Kitab. If you are short of the surah, then recite from where you are short, and do not recite Fatihat al-Kitab.'

He said: 'And it was preferred in it that Surah Al-Kahf and Surah Al-Hijr be recited, unless the imam is one who makes it difficult for those behind him. If you can make your prayer prominent (outdoors) so that a house does not obscure you, then do so. And the prayer of the solar eclipse is longer than the prayer of the lunar eclipse, and they are equal in recitation, bowing, and prostration.'
ai.seo_question: What is the prescribed number of rak'ahs and the specific method for performing the Islamic eclipse prayer?
ai.summary: Transmitted through the chain of Zurara and Muhammad ibn Muslim, this hadith from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* establishes the ten-rak'ah structure of the eclipse prayer, emphasizing the Prophet’s practice of prolonging qunut and recitation. It highlights the scholarly preference for reciting Surah Al-Kahf and Al-Hijr, while distinguishing the solar eclipse prayer as longer in duration than the lunar one, reflecting the cosmic signs' gravity in Shia jurisprudence.
